```{r}
#| label: appendix-inputs
root <- if (dir.exists("results") && dir.exists("R")) "." else ".."
result_path <- function(name) file.path(root, "results", name)
metadata_path <- result_path("run-metadata.rds")
run_metadata <- if (file.exists(metadata_path)) readRDS(metadata_path) else list()
empirical_input <- identical(run_metadata$data_kind, "empirical") &&
  identical(run_metadata$mapping_status, "publication_and_source_labels_verified")
read_empirical <- function(name, required) {
  if (!empirical_input || !file.exists(result_path(name))) return(NULL)
  x <- read.csv(result_path(name), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
  if (!all(required %in% names(x))) stop("Appendix input lacks required fields: ", name)
  if (!nrow(x)) return(NULL)
  x
}
benchmarks <- read_empirical("replication_benchmarks.csv",
  c("table", "sex", "age_sample", "outcome", "statistic", "year", "original_value", "reproduced_value", "tolerance", "passed"))
extensions <- read_empirical("extension.csv", c("sex", "age_sample", "outcome", "window", "method", "estimate"))
support <- read_empirical("overlap.csv", c("sex", "age_sample", "outcome", "window", "cell", "transport_ess", "min_probability_in_target", "target_probability_below_001_share", "density_ratio_min", "density_ratio_max", "max_transport_weight_share"))
bootstrap <- read_empirical("bootstrap.csv", c("outcome", "method", "n_success", "n_requested", "intervals_available"))
stratum_label <- function(sex, age) paste(ifelse(sex == "male", "Men", "Women"), ifelse(age == "young", "21–39", "40–58"))
show_table <- function(x, caption, digits = 3) print(knitr::kable(x, caption = caption, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE))
```

This appendix documents the estimators, assumptions, executed comparisons, and
verification procedures behind the accompanying paper. The acquired source is
the repository author's GitHub release containing SAS data and a checked July
2001 paper proof; it contains no original SAS analysis programs. Publication
descriptions, source labels, and numerical checks support a reconstruction,
with unresolved differences retained. This is not a claim of source-code
equivalence or a verified complete acquisition of the linked Dataverse deposit.
The potential-outcomes framework follows @ding2024. Software tests and numerical
agreement establish different kinds of computational evidence; neither validates
the causal identifying assumptions.

# A common target for four repeated-cross-section cells

Let $G\in\{0,1\}$ denote reported work-limiting disability, $T\in\{0,1\}$ the
pre/post period, $X$ the selected covariates, and $Y$ an annual employment outcome.
Write $A=(G,T)$ and abbreviate its four values by the **two-character cell
labels** $00,01,10,11$, rather than the product $G\times T$. The target cell is
$a^*=11$. Different people
are observed across years, so the analysis never constructs an individual
outcome change from unmatched records.

Let $s_i>0$ be the analysis weight. Within each sex-by-age analysis sample,
the pipeline divides the original survey weight by its year's total and then
by the number of years in that period. Thus years have equal mass within a
period, and the pre and post periods each have total mass one. Survey weights
define the within-year population; this additional normalization declares the
mixture of years. It does not create a panel or a survey-design variance estimator.
The annual descriptive and event-study analyses retain the original relative
survey weights instead.

Use $E_s$ and $P_s$ for expectations and probabilities in this declared weighted
population. Define
$$
q_a(x)=P_s(A=a\mid X=x),\qquad
m_a(x)=E_s[Y\mid A=a,X=x],\qquad p_*=P_s(A=11).
$$
For every source cell, the common-target mean is
$$
\mu_a=E_s[m_a(X)\mid A=11].
$$
The target mean $\mu_{11}=E_s[Y\mid A=11]$ is observed. The statistical estimand is
$$
\theta=\mu_{11}-\mu_{10}-\mu_{01}+\mu_{00}.
$$
All adjusted methods use the same complete-case observations, period windows,
covariates, and disabled-post target. The unadjusted DID is also reported, but
its four raw means average over each cell's own covariate distribution; it is
a descriptive benchmark rather than another estimator of exactly the same
standardized functional when composition differs.

## Transport, standardization, and augmentation

Let $S_*=\sum_i s_i1(A_i=11)$ and
$\widehat r_a(x)=\widehat q_{11}(x)/\widehat q_a(x)$. For a source cell
$a\in\{00,01,10\}$, regression standardization is
$$
\widehat\mu_a^{\mathrm{RA}}
=\frac{1}{S_*}\sum_i s_i1(A_i=11)\widehat m_a(X_i).
$$
The normalized IPW transported mean is
$$
\widehat\mu_a^{\mathrm{IPW}}
=\frac{\sum_i s_i1(A_i=a)\widehat r_a(X_i)Y_i}
        {\sum_i s_i1(A_i=a)\widehat r_a(X_i)}.
$$
The implemented augmented mean instead uses target-mass normalization in its
residual correction:
$$
\widehat\mu_a^{\mathrm{AIPW}}
=\widehat\mu_a^{\mathrm{RA}}
+\frac{1}{S_*}\sum_i s_i1(A_i=a)\widehat r_a(X_i)
                       \{Y_i-\widehat m_a(X_i)\}.
$$
For $a=11$, use the weighted observed mean for all methods. Insert the four
means into the same signed contrast to obtain each adjusted DID. The IPW and
AIPW denominators deliberately differ: replacing $S_*$ by the transported
source mass in the residual term produces a different finite-sample estimator.
Multiplying every $s_i$ by a common positive constant leaves all these estimates
unchanged.

The initial nuisance models are a weighted multinomial logit for the four cell
probabilities and separate weighted linear outcome models in the three source
cells. The primary covariates are centered age, its square, and the historical
recorded race categories, with analyses stratified by recorded sex and age
range. The richer specification additionally adjusts for recorded education
and region. These additional variables are not assumed automatically to be
unaffected by policy. Neither model adjusts for benefits receipt, current
employment, or another realized labor-market outcome as a baseline confounder.

This construction is a common-target transport contrast. It is not presented
as an implementation of the particular repeated-cross-section score in
@santanna2020. That literature and the semiparametric DID framework of
@abadie2005 motivate adjustment under explicit identifying assumptions;
method names alone do not establish those assumptions.

## Why the augmentation is doubly robust

Suppose the fitted source outcome model and density ratio converge to
$\widetilde m_a$ and $\widetilde r_a$, respectively. The population limit of
the augmented source mean is
$$
\widetilde\mu_a
=\frac{E_s[1(A=11)\widetilde m_a(X)]}{p_*}
+\frac{E_s[1(A=a)\widetilde r_a(X)
                  \{Y-\widetilde m_a(X)\}]}{p_*}.
$$
Iterated expectation gives the bias identity
$$
\widetilde\mu_a-\mu_a
=\frac{1}{p_*}E_s\!\left[
\{q_{11}(X)-q_a(X)\widetilde r_a(X)\}
\{\widetilde m_a(X)-m_a(X)\}\right].
$$
The bias vanishes if the source outcome model is correct or the density ratio
is correct. For the full contrast, the condition must hold for **each** of the
three source cells. Merely fitting both models does not guarantee that either
is correct. Consistency also requires support, integrability, and suitable
convergence conditions. Flexible models would require additional attention
to overfitting, cross-fitting, and rates; the current parametric implementation
does not claim those features.

Double robustness concerns estimation of the defined observed-data functional.
It does not make conditional parallel trends true, stabilize changing disability
reporting, or turn a post-policy characteristic into a baseline covariate.

# Conditions for a policy interpretation

Let $G^*$ describe a stable, pre-policy disability group and let $Y_t(p)$ denote
the outcome under policy regime $p\in\{0,1\}$. An ATT-like interpretation of the
standardized contrast requires a link between observed $G$ and this stable
group, as well as the following conditions.

1. **Consistency and a defined exposure.** Recorded outcomes correspond to
   the policy regime received, with an account of phased employer coverage
   and partial exposure. The ADA is the intervention; disability itself is not.
2. **No anticipation in the chosen pre window.** The pre outcomes represent
   the no-policy regime. Passage, implementation, and a first full outcome
   year must not be treated as interchangeable dates.
3. **Conditional parallel untreated changes.** For relevant $x$,
   $$
   E[Y_1(0)-Y_0(0)\mid G^*=1,X=x]
   =E[Y_1(0)-Y_0(0)\mid G^*=0,X=x].
   $$
   Repeated-cross-section sampling must permit identification of the two
   period-specific conditional means for each stable group. The comparison
   also needs a defensible restriction on spillovers or other policy effects
   on the comparison group.
4. **Stable composition and measurement.** Changes in disability reporting,
   sample inclusion, measurement, or unobserved health must not independently
   change the group contrast after adjustment. Conditional standardization
   cannot correct unmeasured changes in who is counted as disabled.
5. **Common support and appropriate covariates.** Every target covariate
   pattern must be supported in all source cells. Covariates used to justify
   identification must be predetermined or otherwise justified, rather than
   chosen only because they improve prediction.

Under these restrictions, the change in the comparison group's untreated
outcomes supplies the missing change for the stable treated group. Without
them, $\theta$ remains a standardized change in observed group disparities.
Survey precision and agreement among RA, IPW, and AIPW cannot distinguish these
interpretations by themselves. Pre-period event-study diagnostics are useful
but have limited power, and selecting an analysis after a pre-trend test can
distort inference [@roth2022].

## Reporting endogeneity as a causal graph

Consider predetermined characteristics $X_0$, underlying health $H_0$, policy
$P$, annual employment $Y_t$, disability reported at a later interview
$G_{t+1}$, and contemporaneous benefits receipt $B_{t+1}$. A plausible graph
includes the following directed paths:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&P\longrightarrow Y_t\longrightarrow G_{t+1},
&&P\longrightarrow G_{t+1},\\
&H_0\longrightarrow Y_t,
&&H_0\longrightarrow G_{t+1},\\
&X_0\longrightarrow H_0,
&&X_0\longrightarrow Y_t,\\
&P\longrightarrow B_{t+1},
&&Y_t\longrightarrow B_{t+1}\longleftarrow H_0.
\end{aligned}
$$
These edges describe threats to assess, not estimated causal relationships.
Indexing employment before interview reporting avoids a simultaneous feedback
cycle. The observed disability group can be a descendant of policy and
employment. Conditioning on it can also select on the collider
$P\rightarrow G_{t+1}\leftarrow H_0$. Benefits receipt is likewise an unsafe
automatic control or sample restriction in this graph. Excluding recipients
can select on employment and health rather than isolate a pure policy effect.

An observed decline in disabled-group employment could therefore reflect
changes in reporting or composition even if the policy's effect on any fixed
person were zero. The contribution of this study is to make that possibility
visible through timing, prevalence, composition, and sensitivity checks, not
to claim that reweighting eliminates it.

# Diagnostics, uncertainty, and resampling

## Support and balance

The initial software draft used 0.01 as a lower bound on fitted four-cell joint
probabilities. Inspection of the acquired data showed that this guard conflated
rare disability-cell prevalence with the covariate support required for
transport. The amended empirical runner uses $10^{-6}$ as a numerical floor
and retains an effective-sample-size minimum of 20. It reports the target-weight
share below 0.01 rather than silently removing those observations. The same
amended rule applies to every empirical stratum, window, outcome, and bootstrap
refit; the generic function's default remains 0.01. The chronology, rationale,
and diagnostic evidence are recorded in `docs/support-amendment.md`.

For transported weights $v_i$, the reported
quantity is $\operatorname{ESS}=(\sum_i v_i)^2/\sum_i v_i^2$; it is a weight
concentration diagnostic, not the number of independent survey clusters.
The maximum normalized weight share and cell sample counts accompany it.
These thresholds are declared computational diagnostics, not universal
criteria for causal validity. Failure stops that specification; the software
does not silently clip probabilities or remove observations.

To separate prevalence from relative covariate support, it also reports
$$
\rho_a(x)=\frac{q_{11}(x)}{q_a(x)}\frac{P_s(A=a)}{P_s(A=11)}
=\frac{f_s(x\mid A=11)}{f_s(x\mid A=a)}.
$$
The fitted joint probabilities, density ratios, ESS, and maximum weight shares
must be assessed together. None tests conditional parallel trends or stable
disability reporting.

Balance compares each donor cell with the same disabled-post target before
and after transport. Standardized differences use the target population's
weighted standard deviation for each model-matrix column. A target-constant
column has an undefined standardized difference and is flagged rather than
treated as perfectly balanced. Balance on included columns cannot demonstrate
balance on unobserved health or validate the counterfactual trend.

## Shared covariance and the meaning of uncertainty

The four estimates share observations through the target distribution,
multinomial model, and nuisance fitting. Their standard errors cannot be added
as though four independent cell means were being combined. For illustration,
with fixed correct nuisances and independent observations, let
$d_*=E[s1(A=11)]$. A source-mean influence contribution takes the form
$$
\phi_a=\frac{s}{d_*}\left[
1(A=11)\{m_a(X)-\mu_a\}
+1(A=a)r_a(X)\{Y-m_a(X)\}\right],
$$
while $\phi_{11}=s1(A=11)(Y-\mu_{11})/d_*$. The contrast contribution is
$\phi_\theta=\phi_{11}-\phi_{10}-\phi_{01}+\phi_{00}$, whose variance includes
all covariances. Estimated nuisance models and a complex sample design require
additional justification; this display is not the implemented variance formula.

The annual event-study intervals use HC1 under an individual-independence
working model. They do not account automatically for CPS rotation, household
dependence, the sample design, or a common national disability-specific shock.
Serial dependence can seriously distort DID uncertainty [@bertrand2004].
There is one national policy timeline, so a large number of survey respondents
does not create many independent policy assignments. Neither a state-cluster
standard error nor the individual bootstrap below can remove a confounding
nationwide trend.

## Implemented bootstrap algorithm

For a fixed outcome, stratum, window, covariate specification, and complete-case
sample, the optional bootstrap proceeds as follows:

1. Fit the point estimator and retain the original analysis weights and the
   observed cell counts $n_{00},n_{01},n_{10},n_{11}$.
2. Within each cell independently, draw $n_a$ rows with replacement. Carry
   each selected row's analysis weight with it. This conditions on the observed
   four cell counts; it does not resample a CPS survey design.
3. Refit the multinomial model and all three source outcome regressions on
   the resampled observations. Recompute the observed target mean, adjustment
   estimates, and support diagnostics. Resampling only precomputed treatment
   effects or holding the fitted nuisances fixed would omit uncertainty.
4. Repeat using the recorded seed. Save every replicate's status and any
   failure reason. By default, **all requested replicates must succeed** before
   bootstrap standard errors or intervals are reported. An explicitly relaxed
   success requirement is labeled as inference conditional on successful
   replicates, not silently substituted for the default.
5. For an eligible run, report the replicate standard deviation and the 2.5th
   and 97.5th percentiles using R's type-7 quantile convention. Runs with fewer
   than 199 replicates are labeled exploratory. Even 199 replicates gives
   limited tail resolution; more draws address Monte Carlo error, not a wrong
   sampling or identification model.

Reproducible parallel execution assigns a seed to each replicate before
dispatch. The serial and parallel implementations therefore produce the same
draws and results for a fixed seed. Multinomial fitting combines identical
covariate/cell rows by summing their weights, an exact likelihood reduction;
no respondent subsample replaces the declared empirical population.

The main pipeline requests this procedure for the primary-window weeks-worked
and any-work analyses in each of the four sex-by-age strata. The bootstrap
conditions on the supplied period/year analysis weights rather than rebuilding
their original survey totals in every draw. These intervals are therefore
conditional sampling summaries. A final design-based analysis requires the
actual archive's household/PSU/stratum information or appropriate replicate
weights and a resampling method consistent with them.

# Distributional and trend sensitivity extensions

## Threshold outcomes are not quantile treatment effects

For $k\in\{0,13,26,39,51\}$, define
$Y_k=1(\mathrm{weeks}\leq k)$. The same four-cell method estimates
$$
\theta_k=F_{11}^*(k)-F_{10}^*(k)-F_{01}^*(k)+F_{00}^*(k),
$$
where $F_a^*(k)$ is the source cell's cumulative employment distribution
standardized to the disabled-post target. At $k=0$, the outcome is no weeks
worked; higher thresholds examine changes in the share with relatively little
annual employment. A positive $\theta_k$ is an increase in the cumulative
probability contrast, not an increase in weeks worked. Since the samples are
the same and the estimator is linear in the outcome, the zero-weeks contrast
is the negative of the any-work contrast, up to numerical precision.

A causal distributional interpretation requires parallel trends for the
threshold indicators, which does not follow from parallel trends in mean
weeks. These contrasts neither identify individual rank preservation nor
quantile treatment effects. The implied counterfactual CDF need not satisfy
range and monotonicity restrictions under arbitrary data and models; it should
not be inverted mechanically. Thresholds are prespecified, and a collection
of pointwise comparisons must not be described as a simultaneous confidence
band. The current distributional output is a diagnostic point-estimate
extension, not a quantified causal distributional claim.

## Exact linear loading for the implemented bias curve

Let $\mathcal L(Y)$ denote the fitted AIPW contrast for fixed observations,
weights, covariates, and cell-probability estimates. Because the source outcome
fits are weighted linear regressions with fixed design matrices, this estimator
is linear in $Y$. Define
$$
H_i=G_i(\mathrm{outcome\_year}_i-1987),\qquad
L=\mathcal L(H),\qquad \widehat\theta=\mathcal L(Y).
$$
For a hypothetical differential untreated drift of $b$ outcome units per year,
the outcome perturbation $Y_i^{(b)}=Y_i-bH_i$ gives the exact fitted-model identity
$$
\mathcal L(Y^{(b)})=\widehat\theta-bL.
$$
The pipeline computes $L$ by running the **same estimator** on $H$. It is not
replaced by the arithmetic difference between mean pre and post years: common
target standardization and estimated residual corrections can change that
loading. The output column named `year_separation` stores this estimator
loading. With $L\neq0$, the drift that moves the point contrast to zero is
$b_0=\widehat\theta/L$; it is undefined when the loading vanishes.

The declared grid is $b=-1,-0.75,\ldots,1$ weeks per year for weeks worked and
$b=-0.02,-0.015,\ldots,0.02$ probability units per year for any work. Applying
this algebra to a binary outcome is a bias sensitivity calculation, not a
claim that every perturbed value is a realizable binary observation. Holding
the sample and nuisance designs fixed is essential to the identity. Tests
compare the shortcut against direct outcome-perturbation refits.

This is a one-dimensional, linear trend-bias model. It is not a general
identification region, a simultaneous sensitivity interval, or an implementation
of the robust trend restrictions in @rambachan2023. Its role is to put the
counterfactual trend required to explain the point estimate on an interpretable
scale. Sampling uncertainty and uncertainty about $b$ remain distinct.

# Executed reconstruction and additional results

## Scope of the numerical comparison

The supplied SAS extract contains 971,058 records. Age eligibility retains
759,771; excluding missing or zero `FNLWGT2` leaves 709,125 weighted estimation
records. Table 1's printed observation counts refer to the raw age-eligible
population, whereas its weighted means and the regressions use valid weights.
Keeping these populations separate reconciles all 40 selected Table 1 counts
and all eight Table 2 estimation counts. Original weight-construction programs
are absent, so the precise historical reason for each excluded weight is not
asserted.

The reconstructed Table 2 no-trend model uses outcome-year 1987 as the reference,
full categorical demographic controls, and year-by-demographic interactions.
This differs from the extension's age-polynomial event-study model. Its
conventional WLS covariance is reported as the reconstruction convention;
the extension's HC1 and bootstrap uncertainty have different interpretations.
The benchmark source is the supplied July 2001 proof, not an independently
retrieved final printing. Proof/PDF pages 13–14 contain Table 1, and page 17
contains Table 2.

```{r}
#| label: benchmark-summary
#| results: asis
if (is.null(benchmarks)) {
  cat("**Executed benchmark comparisons are unavailable in this render.**\n")
} else {
  if (anyNA(benchmarks$passed) || any(!is.finite(as.matrix(benchmarks[c("original_value", "reproduced_value", "tolerance")])))) stop("Invalid empirical benchmark values")
  matched <- sum(benchmarks$passed)
  cat(sprintf("The executed comparison matches **%d of %d selected entries** at their declared printed-precision tolerances. **%d discrepancies remain**; they are retained below rather than relabeled as passes. The selection covers Table 1 age/weekly-employment means and counts, and Table 2 no-trend employment/log-wage coefficients, standard errors, and counts. It does not cover every original table or the trend columns.\n", matched, nrow(benchmarks), nrow(benchmarks)-matched))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: benchmark-discrepancies
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(benchmarks)) {
  x <- benchmarks[!benchmarks$passed, ]
  if (nrow(x)) {
    short_stratum <- paste0(ifelse(x$sex == "male", "M", "F"), ifelse(x$age_sample == "young", "21–39", "40–58"))
    label <- paste(sub("Table ", "T", x$table), short_stratum,
      ifelse(x$outcome == "weeks", "weeks", "log wage"),
      ifelse(x$statistic == "std_error", "SE", ifelse(x$statistic == "coefficient", "coef.", "mean")))
    show_table(data.frame(Comparison = label, Year = x$year, Printed = x$original_value,
      Reconstructed = x$reproduced_value, Tolerance = x$tolerance),
      "All retained discrepancies. T1 uses survey years; T2 uses outcome years. M/F denote recorded male/female strata.", digits = 6)
  }
}
```

`docs/replication-audit.md` records the complete comparison rules, source
transcription, and independent checks. All 36 selected Table 2 employment
coefficients match the source precision. The disputed older-male 1988 weeks
standard error and young-female 1992 wage coefficient were also reproduced by
independent `stats::lm` fits on the actual samples. These checks make a
package-specific numerical error less likely, but do not establish that the
proof's values are typographical errors. The differences remain unresolved
without original programs, execution logs, or another verified source version.

## All prespecified period windows

The following table reports the AIPW contrast for every declared stratum and
period window. It complements the main paper's method comparison. The bootstrap
applies to the primary window; alternative windows here are point comparisons.
Probability
contrasts are multiplied by 100 to express percentage points. These point
contrasts do not become policy effects solely because several windows have
the same sign; older women's pre-period trend remains a particularly relevant
counterexample to that argument.

```{r}
#| label: all-window-aipw
#| results: asis
if (is.null(extensions)) {
  cat("**Executed extension estimates are unavailable in this render.**\n")
} else {
  x <- extensions[extensions$method == "aipw_standardized_did", ]
  w <- x[x$outcome == "weeks", c("sex", "age_sample", "window", "estimate")]
  p <- x[x$outcome == "worked_any", c("sex", "age_sample", "window", "estimate")]
  names(w)[4] <- "weeks"; names(p)[4] <- "probability"
  x <- merge(w, p, by = c("sex", "age_sample", "window"), all = TRUE)
  x <- x[order(factor(x$sex, levels=c("male", "female")), factor(x$age_sample, levels=c("young", "old")), factor(x$window, levels=c("main", "later_coverage", "broader_pre"))), ]
  period_labels <- c(main="1987–89 / 1993–96", later_coverage="1987–89 / 1995–96", broader_pre="1987–91 / 1993–96")
  show_table(data.frame(Stratum = stratum_label(x$sex,x$age_sample),
    `Pre / post years` = unname(period_labels[x$window]), Weeks = x$weeks,
    `Any work (pp)` = 100*x$probability, check.names=FALSE),
    "AIPW standardized group-disparity changes across all prespecified outcome-year windows.")
}
```

## Observed support in the primary window

```{r}
#| label: support-evidence
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(support)) {
  x <- support[support$window == "main" & support$outcome == "weeks", ]
  split_x <- split(x, interaction(x$sex, x$age_sample, drop=TRUE))
  table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split_x, function(z) data.frame(
    Stratum = stratum_label(z$sex[1],z$age_sample[1]),
    `Min. q` = min(z$min_probability_in_target),
    `Flagged (%)` = 100*max(z$target_probability_below_001_share),
    `Min. ESS` = as.integer(round(min(z$transport_ess))),
    `Ratio range` = sprintf("%.2f–%.2f",min(z$density_ratio_min),max(z$density_ratio_max)),
    `Max. w (%)` = 100*max(z$max_transport_weight_share),check.names=FALSE)))
  table <- table[match(c("Men 21–39","Men 40–58","Women 21–39","Women 40–58"),table$Stratum), ]
  show_table(table,"Primary-window support diagnostics across the four cells within each stratum.",digits=3)
}
```

“Flagged” is the largest, across source cells, target-weight share for which
that cell's joint probability is below the initial 0.01 guard; it is not a
count of excluded observations. The density-ratio range removes the marginal
cell-prevalence factor. The full population is retained under the documented
amendment, with no trimming or probability clipping. The amendment is disclosed
because replacing an initial rule after seeing the source is a design decision,
even when it is motivated by support diagnostics rather than effect estimates.

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap-status
#| results: asis
if (is.null(bootstrap)) {
  cat("**Bootstrap execution is not yet attached to this render.** Point estimates above must not be read as completed inference.\n")
} else {
  b <- bootstrap[bootstrap$method == "aipw_standardized_did", ]
  if (nrow(b) && all(b$intervals_available) && all(b$n_success == b$n_requested)) {
    draw_range <- if (min(b$n_success) == max(b$n_success)) as.character(min(b$n_success)) else sprintf("%d–%d", min(b$n_success), max(b$n_success))
    cat(sprintf("The saved primary-window bootstrap summaries contain %d stratum/outcome AIPW analyses, with %s successful draws each and all requested draws successful. Their intervals remain conditional sampling summaries under the algorithm above, not CPS design-based or national-policy uncertainty.\n", nrow(b), draw_range))
  } else cat("**Bootstrap summaries are partial or have unavailable intervals.** The saved failures and counts must be reviewed before interpreting uncertainty.\n")
}
```

# Source verification and reproducibility

## Mapping verification matrix

The matrix distinguishes verified source/publication evidence from remaining
limits. The source audit is hash-bound in `data/source-verification.json` and
described in `docs/source-audit.md`. Numerical comparison is a separate
verification layer; neither audit supplies the missing original programs.

| Source item | Current implemented rule | Evidence and remaining limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File and format | Supplied SAS file, loaded with Haven | Archive inventory and hashes checked; no original programs or complete-Dataverse claim |
| Year | Survey year 1988–1997; outcome year one less | Source labels and proof pp. 11–12 agree |
| Population | Survey-age 21–58; strata at 40 | Source ranges and all 48 selected population/estimation counts agree |
| Disability | Binary `DISABL1` | Equals `DIS_HP==1` in the supplied records; interview timing and legal coverage remain distinct |
| Weights | Positive `FNLWGT2` / 100 | Counts and numerical agreement support mapping; original reweighting code and reasons for each missing/zero weight unavailable |
| Employment | `WKSWORK` 0–52; zeros retained | Source label specifies last year; no missing weeks in the supplied file |
| Race | Source codes 3–5 pooled | Matches historical three-category specification; coding does not establish group comparability over time |
| Schooling and region | Three schooling groups, nine divisions | Flags verified complete/exclusive; categories reconcile the historical 162-cell definition |
| Earnings | Positive wages/weeks; explicit legacy trimming | All four wage-model counts agree; original CPI and selection programming cannot be inspected |
| Benchmarks | Independently transcribed proof targets | 272 executed comparisons; discrepancies retained; final publisher printing not independently checked |

: Source/publication verification and its remaining limits.

Faithful replication additionally requires matching sample counts, weighted
means, omitted categories, formulas, and variance calculations for explicitly
selected original specifications [@acemoglu2001]. Modernized modeling choices
must be reported as extensions. A match in coefficient signs is not a
replication criterion.

## Commands and artifact boundaries

Run commands from the repository root after environment activation. The first
block works without empirical input and validates software/report behavior:

```bash
source /workspace/stat256-environment/activate.sh
cd /workspace/Stat-256-Final-Project
make test
quarto render --to html
quarto render --to pdf
```

To retrieve the same supplied GitHub release archive:

```bash
make fetch
```

The source audit documents the available paper/data evidence and absent programs.
The following interface runs the empirical pipeline on the verified SAS input:

```bash
Rscript scripts/run_analysis.R /absolute/path/to/marcps_w.sas7bdat \
  --bootstrap 199 --seed 256
quarto render --to html
quarto render --to pdf
```

The downloader records source metadata and checksums; originals remain under
`data/raw/`. Derived observations and analysis artifacts are generated in
`data/derived/` and `results/`. The paper and this appendix render to
`_output/report/` as separate HTML and PDF documents. The software test fixtures
live in temporary directories and must never populate research results.
Retain run metadata, session information, source hashes, version-control state,
and bootstrap success/failure records with any released empirical output.

`make analyze` runs the point estimates and diagnostics; `make analyze-full`
adds the requested bootstrap. If a core or extension check fails, diagnose it
and disclose the failed specification rather than substituting another
window, trimming rule, or synthetic input. Publication requires source
verification, a completed replication comparison that retains any discrepancies,
executed empirical outputs, examined diagnostics, and interpretation written
from those outputs.
